author: dataker
cardQuote: I see it as nothing but an asset mgt company that hired some developers to "prop it up".
quote: Wealthfront markets itself as an innovative fintech startup, but I see it as nothing but an asset mgt company that hired some developers to "prop it up". Not to commit an ad hominem, but I don't see tech-driven founders and/or a very strong engineering culture. https://www.wealthfront.com/management
storyTitle: Wealthfront: Silicon Valley Tech at Wall Street Prices
outcome: Reached roughly $100B in platform assets, 1.5M clients, and completed an IPO in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Wealthfront grew from a robo-advisor into a cash-management and investing platform with $94B in platform assets at the end of FY2026. It listed on Nasdaq in December 2025 at a roughly $2.05B valuation.
note: Calling Wealthfront 'nothing but an asset manager' underestimated the software distribution engine. It kept compounding assets and became a public company, though its IPO valued it at only about $2B.

author: 7Figures2Commas
cardQuote: Bitcoin itself is about as interesting as the Burmese kyat or Gambian dalasi.
quote: > Yeah, another to way to put it is they aim for legitimacy so they can be the bitcoin counterparty of choice for Fortune 500s and wall street. According to Coinbase, the total value of all Bitcoin is currently about $3.5 billion. This is a tiny, tiny market for "Fortune 500s and Wall Street" and is equivalent to the value of a single (smaller) mid-cap company. Even at its peak, the total value of all Bitcoin was only around $14 billion. Daily Bitcoin transaction volume hasn't exceeded $100 million since July and has been as low as $33 million recently[1]. For comparison, daily volume in the FX markets exceeds $5 trillion. Blockchain technology might be important but Bitcoin itself is about as interesting as the Burmese kyat or Gambian dalasi. [1] https://blockchain.info/charts/estimated-transaction-volume-...
outcome: IPO'd on Nasdaq in September 2025 at a $3.3B valuation.
outcomeDetail: Gemini priced its IPO at $28 per share, raised $425M, and began trading as GEMI. The listing valued the exchange at about $3.3B, even as it remained loss-making.
note: The critic correctly noted Bitcoin was small in 2015 but wrongly treated that as a permanent ceiling. Crypto's market grew by orders of magnitude, and Gemini rode it to a public listing.

author: DeBraid
cardQuote: farmers' markets, etc). tldr: Long Shopify, short Square.
quote: > To me the biggest question is what, exactly, Square does? Years ago they were the company that made it easy for people to accept credit card payments who otherwise wouldn't want to / be able to (mom & pop stores, farmers' markets, etc). tldr: Long Shopify, short Square.
storyTitle: Square’s IPO Terms Put Valuation Below Latest Funding Round
outcome: Became Block, a $50B+ public company with 60M Cash App users.
outcomeDetail: Square renamed itself Block in 2021; Square handles merchant payments while Cash App reached 60 million monthly transacting users. Block's market cap was roughly $52B in late 2026, and it remained profitable.
note: The one-line short call missed Square's expansion into consumer finance. Cash App became the growth engine, and Square's merchant base proved stickier than the 'mom and pop' framing suggested.

author: mikemac
cardQuote: There is zero chance I'd subject employees to a hacked together payroll system.
quote: > a free product that performs the most important function of their very expensive product line There is zero chance I'd subject employees to a hacked together payroll system. Building one is far from trivial, considering the complexities of tax and employment law in 50 different states.
storyTitle: Zenefits launches free payroll software for small businesses
outcome: Slashed its valuation from $4.5B to $2B and was sold to TriNet for about $209M, but the product still operates.
outcomeDetail: Zenefits was valued at $4.5B in 2015, then a licensing scandal forced CEO Parker Conrad out in 2016 and the company repriced itself at $2B. TriNet acquired it in 2022 for about $209M.
note: The warning that payroll is hard to bolt on was right. Zenefits’ free-payroll push papered over compliance and service problems, and the company never recovered its early valuation — but it did not shut down.

author: polishninja
cardQuote: Better software can only get you so far in banking.
quote: Better software can only get you so far in banking. At the end of the day, they need to borrow and loan profitability and provide services at a low cost. In addition, they need customers, which are not easy to acquire for a new bank. Not having physical branches is definitely a cost saver; however, I’ve seen some surveys that indicate people still want access to some sort of physical branch. According to their previous Techcrunch article [0], they are writing their own full-stack banking software. Writing your own banking core, external facing software, and internal process software is a massive undertaking, especially dealing with all the regulation and certification processes with third parties. You then become not only a bank but a specialized software development shop as well. Something traditionally only the big banks can afford. I’m not sure, given they are a bank and software business, that their cost base is 1% or 2% of a traditional bank, as stated in their article [0]. I hope they build something awesome but I think to do something of this size will take more than a few million. Disclaimer: I write banking software. [0] http://techcrunch.com/2015/06/30/mondo-gets-passionate/
storyTitle: Startup bank Mondo raised £1m crowdfunding in 96 seconds
outcome: Grew to more than 12 million UK customers, posted a profit, and was valued at $5.9B.
outcomeDetail: Monzo became one of Britain's largest digital banks, with over 12 million customers and £1.2B of revenue in FY2025. It reported a £60.4M pre-tax profit and a $5.9B valuation in a 2024 secondary sale, and is preparing a London IPO.
note: The critic was right that banking is hard and capital-intensive, but wrong that Monzo's software-first model could not reach scale. Monzo built its own core, won primary-account customers, and turned profitable.

author: JSONwebtoken
cardQuote: the path to a $4 billion tech valuation with no actual tech product.
quote: Sunk cost fallacy. Investors put in $100 million in 2011 when the mere concept of Fintech would give venture capitalists chubs. Back then, it wasn't so clear that millennials and personal finance are like water and oil -- and that you would need more than a landing page and a webform to drive organic growth. SoFi would also feed investors both false information (as mentioned in the article), and inflated user growth numbers fueled by their freedom as a "startup" to spend insane amounts of money on customer acquisition with no regard for profitability. Basically, SoFi spent all their money convincing people through advertising that they were "a new kind of finance company", all without actually creating anything new. Turns out the company stops growing if you stop giving them money, and VCs didn't want to lose their $100 million commitment or admit that the company was DoA, so along came more rounds of funding. There you go, that's the path to a $4 billion tech valuation with no actual tech product.
storyTitle: The Sex Scandal That Toppled SoFi’s C.E.O
outcome: Went public in 2021, obtained a national bank charter, and reached 17M members.
outcomeDetail: SoFi merged with a SPAC in 2021, acquired a national bank charter in 2022, and grew to 17.1 million members by Q3 2026. It reported record net revenue of $1.4B and $241M of net income that quarter.
note: The critic saw a lead-generation webform; SoFi became a chartered bank with a large deposit base. Its 2017 scandal was real, but it did not prevent the franchise from scaling.

author: valdiorn
cardQuote: Upgrade a 750 million dollar a day trading system with no rollback strategy. Amateur hour
quote: Upgrade a 750 million dollar a day trading system with no rollback strategy. Amateur hour, and if this were a "real" exchange, they'd lose their licence and have lawsuits and government agents knocking down their door (real-money MTFs have strict uptime and infrastructure requirements for anyone who didn't know)
storyTitle: Kraken Goes Down for 40 Hours, Drawing Mt. Gox Comparisons
outcome: Became one of the largest crypto exchanges, valued at $20B in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Kraken recovered from the 2018 outage, acquired NinjaTrader for $1.5B, and raised at a $20B valuation in November 2025. It generated an estimated $2.2B of revenue in 2025 and was preparing an IPO.
note: The outage was a real operational failure, but 'amateur hour' did not sink Kraken. It professionalized, consolidated the market, and became one of the sector's most valuable private companies.

author: shaqbert
cardQuote: The key issue with N26 is their poor unit economics. Right now, they are losing money on most of the checking accounts
quote: The key issue with N26 is their poor unit economics. Right now, they are losing money on most of the checking accounts, as they foot the ATM wholesale fee (though they limit it to 3 "free" ATM withdrawals per months). The issue is that they don't have enough premium services to compensate for the "loss leader" like regular banks do. The hope from Tencent and Allianz is that they will add these now, and then move to great unit economics, but for now they are bleeding red ink.
storyTitle: N26 raises $160M from Tencent and Allianz
outcome: Reached a $9B valuation and millions of customers, then retrenched from the UK and US.
outcomeDetail: N26 raised $900M at a $9B valuation in 2021 and expanded across Europe. It later exited the UK and US, cut costs, and its valuation reportedly fell to about $3B by 2026, though it reported its first full-year profit.
note: The unit-economics warning was prescient: N26's growth was expensive and its global expansion stalled. It survived and became profitable, but at a much lower valuation than its peak.

author: soared
cardQuote: I don't understand how connecting to my bank account provides 10-20x more credit
quote: How is this different from a, for example, chase business credit card (or debit card for that matter)? If you have funding but no credit history you can get one. I was 19 when I got mine. I don't understand how connecting to my bank account provides 10-20x more credit if you're already verifying my startup's funding.
storyTitle: Launch HN: Brex (YC W17) – Corporate Credit Card for Startups
outcome: Reached a $12.3B private valuation and was acquired by Capital One for $5.15B.
outcomeDetail: Brex scaled corporate cards and spend management to thousands of startups, peaking at a $12.3B valuation in 2022. Capital One agreed to buy it in January 2026 for $5.15B, a steep discount to that peak but a major exit.
note: The 'how is this different from a Chase business card' critique missed the underwriting innovation: Brex underwrote startups on cash balances and investor backing, not personal guarantees. That created a durable niche.

author: runako
cardQuote: is there ever a compelling reason to not wait a few years for the bank to smooth out its operations
quote: So far, I'm intrigued. But I'm also conservative when it comes to money. None of these questions are specific to Mercury, they are general to any of the fintech startups that have been popping up lately. So: - do people really use new banks like this? - how worried is it reasonable to be that bugs in the platform will cause interruption of business/money loss for customers? (I'd be particularly worried that I wouldn't immediately catch an error in the bank's favor.) - in general, is there ever a compelling reason to not wait a few years for the bank to smooth out its operations before getting on board? All that said, I love to see innovation in the space and it looks like a refreshing start!
outcome: Reached 200,000+ business customers, $650M annualized revenue, and a $3.5B valuation.
outcomeDetail: Mercury grew into a profitable business-banking platform for startups, reporting $500M of revenue in 2024 and $650M of annualized revenue by Q3 2025. It raised a $300M Series C at a $3.5B valuation in 2025.
note: The caution about waiting a few years was reasonable, but Mercury's timing was good: it picked up deposits after SVB's collapse, stayed profitable, and became a serious alternative to legacy business banks.

author: Peroni
cardQuote: They live by the mantra of move fast and break things. That mantra is inevitably going to cause problems when your entire business is dealing with real money
quote: Revolut's CFO recently 'resigned' from the company in light of claims that Revolut switched off an anti-money laundering system that flags suspect transactions. Revolut cited 'personal and health reasons' for the CFO's resignation. Whatever those personal and health reasons really were, they clearly passed quite quickly as within the space of a few weeks, said CFO has joined another FinTech company as their new CFO. The company quite literally has the words "get sh*t done" in giant neon letters on their office wall. They live by the mantra of move fast and break things. That mantra is inevitably going to cause problems when your entire business is dealing with real money owned by real people in one of the most heavily regulated industries in the world.
storyTitle: I just had over a thousand Euros stolen and Revolut is siding with the thief
outcome: Reached 65M+ customers and a $75B valuation despite recurring AML problems.
outcomeDetail: Revolut grew into Europe's most valuable private fintech, with more than 65 million customers and $4B of 2024 revenue. It was valued at $75B in a November 2025 share sale, even after earlier AML and compliance controversies.
note: The critique of 'move fast and break things' in banking was fair, and Revolut did have repeated compliance problems. But the culture that worried the critic also produced relentless product expansion and growth.

author: ryanmercer
cardQuote: I truly don't understand why a payroll company would need to raise 200 million dollars
quote: I truly don't understand why a payroll company would need to raise 200 million dollars and what they could possibly do with the bulk of it aside from buying 24k gold toilets. You're not going to hire 200 million worth of people, or buy that many ads, you could build your own server farm for a fraction of that and cloud services would take quite a long time to burn through that. So why? Why would you sell that much of your company to investors? Why would you invest that much money in a payroll company? I can sometimes understand it, say a company was working on some sort of energy generation and needed tens of millions of dollars of equipment/infrastructure to even start truly testing their idea, or you were going to sell some physical good that was going to sell for hundreds or thousands of dollars per unit and you've already been selling other versions but need a large amount of cash for the MOQ to manufacture your new hardware in the best setting and banks are hesitant to pony up, but for a payroll company?! This stuff always blows my mind.
outcome: Valued at $9.3B and acquired Guideline to expand into retirement benefits.
outcomeDetail: Gusto grew into a payroll, benefits, and HR platform serving more than 400,000 small businesses. It was valued at $9.3B in a 2025 tender offer and bought Guideline, a 401(k) provider, for a reported $600M.
note: The '$200M for a payroll company' reaction underestimated how much capital and engineering it takes to run payroll across states. Gusto turned a boring compliance product into a durable, cash-generating platform.

author: aguyfromnb
cardQuote: Bill.com is not Amazon.com. That's a theory , a selling-point, and it comes from "Silicon Valley" itself.
quote: > With those kinds of numbers they can invest less in customer acquisition and turn on the money tap any time they want. Where does this notion come from that these companies can "make money whenever they want", but haven't done so in a decade or more? People point to Amazon as an analogy all the time: it took Amazon about 5 years to make a profit, and this was the early internet. Bill.com is not Amazon.com. That's a theory , a selling-point, and it comes from "Silicon Valley" itself. In reality, the growth tends to come from the customer acquisition spend, and growth will likely cease the minute customer acquisition spending stops. Growth is already slowing down, and this company has never made a dime. So what value do you put on it now? Where does the idea assumption from that these companies are "putting profits back into the company"? That money has to show up in the financials statements as well, it's not magic.
outcome: Reached $1.5B in annual revenue and $240M in non-GAAP operating income.
outcomeDetail: Bill.com IPO'd in 2019 and became a leading accounts-payable platform for small and midsize businesses. In FY2025 it reported $1.46B in revenue, $240M of non-GAAP operating income, and more than 1% of U.S. GDP flowing through its network.
note: The critic was right that Bill.com was not Amazon and that growth was acquisition-driven. But the company proved the model could generate real profits at scale, even if its growth rate normalized.

author: dimmke
cardQuote: I'd love to see one of these fintech startups actually last and not get acquired or turn into a way to market to consumers but it's looking pretty grim.
quote: I used to like these kind of bank startups because they usually have a much more polished user interface/well designed app, but they definitely do stuff like this. Simple was the first big one. Then they got acquired. Then shut down. I switched to a bank called N26 that after 2 months flagged my account for "suspicious activity" and asked me to reupload identification documents. They rejected every single attempt I tried then shut down my account. I then do some reading and turns out they do this to a ton of people. Having a fancy looking debit card and a nice app isn't worth the drama. I'd love to see one of these fintech startups actually last and not get acquired or turn into a way to market to consumers but it's looking pretty grim.
storyTitle: Chime has been suddenly closing accounts, not returning customers’ money
outcome: IPO'd on Nasdaq in June 2025 at an $11.6B valuation.
outcomeDetail: Chime priced its IPO at $27 per share, raised $864M, and closed its first trading day up 37%. The listing valued the company at $11.6B, below its $25B private peak but still one of the largest U.S. fintech IPOs in years.
note: The account-closure story was a genuine consumer-protection problem, but 'these fintech startups won't last' was too broad. Chime reached public markets with millions of users and positive adjusted profitability.

author: purplepatrick
cardQuote: Brex already tried that in the beginning. That’s really only a thing for businesses so small that they definitely do not need a corporate credit card
quote: Remarkable — all that without explaining anywhere what a “corporate card” is. Is it a debit card (debits immediately)? Or a delayed debit card (debits at month end)? Or a credit card (credit balance up to a specified limit)? And why do they brag about “no credit checks”? Brex already tried that in the beginning. That’s really only a thing for businesses so small that they definitely do not need a corporate credit card (and who are bad at picking banks). I scaled a startup to 100 people and had 0 need for issuing cards to employees… But all of these companies seems to do really well, so there must be plenty of demand…
outcome: Became the most valuable spend-management startup, valued at $32B in 2025.
outcomeDetail: Ramp expanded from corporate cards into procurement, travel, and treasury software, passing $1B in annualized revenue. Its valuation rose from $13B to $32B during 2025, with more than 50,000 customers.
note: The dismissal of 'no credit checks' as a niche for tiny businesses missed the market Ramp was building. Startups wanted fast, software-native spend controls, and Ramp sold that into companies of every size.

author: sbierwagen
cardQuote: When Ponzi schemes evaporate, the money disappears.
quote: That is a much worse risk than basically any other investment! If you buy gold, the price will fluctuate, but it won't be lost. If you bought the Dow at the peak in 1929 and held it all the way to the bottom then you lost 89% of your money, but it didn't actually go to zero. When Ponzi schemes evaporate, the money disappears. You can sign on to whatever class action lawsuit comes out of it, but the lawyers are going to eat most of the proceeds. It's more options trading than "investing", and Robinhood's profits demonstrate that most people lose money on options. Blockfi's yields remind me of money market funds in 2008. They looked like bank accounts, and paid out mostly sane yields, but the fine print said "not a bank account, may evaporate". Well, when it threatened to evaporate, everyone freaked out: https://www.investopedia.com/articles/economics/09/money-mar... When the NFT staking people are advertising yields of 132%, https://twitter.com/Route2FI/status/1492940519965605890 that's a huge blinking red sign that says SCAM SCAM SCAM, but 9.25% isn't as big of a warning as it should be. The moral hazard of every market bubble is sophisticated actors chasing yield on the way up, then claiming you were swindled, bamboozled, and had no idea what you were getting into, and urgently need a bailout when the bubble pops.
storyTitle: Blockfi agrees to pay $100M in penalties and pursue registration
outcome: Filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in November 2022.
outcomeDetail: BlockFi froze withdrawals after FTX's collapse and filed for bankruptcy on Nov. 28, 2022, listing between $1B and $10B in assets and liabilities. The SEC had already fined it $100M for selling an unregistered lending product and misleading investors about risk.
note: The comment identified the core problem: yields that looked like a bank account but depended on risky, opaque crypto lending. When the credit cycle turned, BlockFi's promised 9.25% evaporated and customers were locked out.
